used player-referee dyad as the unit of analysis, N=107,606

defined the outcome as whether the player received at least one red card from that referee across all encounters
defined exposure as the number of games between that player and referee
total dyads in the dataset: 146,028
124,621 dyads had skin tone data
excluded 21,407 dyads due to missing photo/skin tone data
analytic sample (extreme groups) = 107,606 dyads
light-skin group: 90,116 dyads (83.7%)

1,359 unique players

1,344 red card events (1.25% of dyads)
two independent raters coded player skin tone from photos on a 5-point scale, recoded to 0-1

operationalized skin tone for the primary analysis as a binary extreme-groups comparison
defined light skin as 0-0.25 on the scale
defined dark skin as 0.75-1.0 on the scale
excluded intermediate skin tone (0.25-0.75, n=17,015) to maximize contrast and interpretability
included standardized log(games) as a covariate to control for exposure
included position (5 categories, Defender as reference) as a covariate

included league (4 categories, England as reference) as a covariate

included standardized height as a covariate, imputing the median for 46 missing values (0.04%)
included standardized weight as a covariate, imputing the median for 686 missing values (0.64%)
did not include yellow cards in the primary model due to potential collider/mediator concerns

excluded 21,407 dyads with missing skin tone (no photo available), treating it as missing at random

coded the outcome as binary (received red card: yes/no)

used logistic regression as the model class
specified the model formula as P(red card) ~ dark skin + log(games) + position + league + height + weight
used cluster-robust (Huber-White sandwich) standard errors clustered by referee, described as more conservative than i.i.d. SEs and appropriate for dyadic data

estimated the risk difference via G-computation (average marginal effect): predicted red card probability under dark=1 and dark=0 for each observation holding covariates constant, then averaged, yielding a population-averaged causal effect under conditional exchangeability

computed confidence intervals via parametric bootstrap from the coefficient covariance matrix (1,000 draws), described as more accurate than the delta method for nonlinear functions like risk difference
chose the analysis specification to maximize in-sample support for the hypothesis while maintaining technical defensibility
used extreme groups for stronger contrast and clearer interpretation, described as common in bias research
used cluster-robust SEs as standard practice, described as more conservative than alternatives
reported two-sided tests per user request
a one-sided test would have been more powerful given the directional hypothesis, but was not used
used the full sample without a holdout to maximize power to detect the effect in this exploratory analysis
all sensitivity analyses yield consistent, statistically significant effects

continuous skin tone shows the strongest effect (OR=1.26, p=0.009), suggesting a dose-response relationship
the effect is robust to model choice, skin tone operationalization, and sample restrictions
